description: AgriSpectra aims to transform NASA Earth observation data into practical tools for climate-resilient farming. We combine agriculture, data analysis, and Operations Research to develop innovative decision-support solutions for sustainable crop rotation. We welcome motivated teammates with skills in Python, GIS, remote sensing, agronomy, AI, and web development. Join us to turn space data into smarter, more sustainable farming decisions!!!
summary: AgriSpectra is an interactive agricultural decision-support application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It combines NASA POWER historical climate data, a transparent three-year economic comparison, and farmers’ own assessments of agricultural cost relationships using DEMATEL. Focusing on maize cultivation in the Nestos Valley, Kavala, Greece, it explores continuous maize, maize–wheat rotation and maize with winter vetch as green manure. By bringing climate evidence, economic assumptions, and local experience into one accessible interface, AgriSpectra helps farmers explore more informed, climate-aware cropping decisions without claiming to predict yields or future profits.
details: AgriSpectra is an R Shiny web application designed as a pilot decision-support tool for maize-based cropping systems in the Nestos Valley, Kavala, Greece. It compares three illustrative strategies over a common three-year horizon: (A) continuous maize cultivation; (B) a maize–winter wheat sequence, with maize returning in the third year; and (C) maize with winter common vetch used as green manure. The calendars are indicative and require local agronomic verification. The economic module lets users enter cultivated area, crop yields, selling prices, and production costs. It calculates illustrative total net results for each strategy over three years and identifies the strategy with the highest estimated net result under the entered assumptions. A sensitivity analysis explores how changes in yields, prices, and costs affect these comparisons. These are scenario calculations, not yield or profit forecasts. The climate module uses NASA POWER daily historical data for 1991–2025 at the pilot location. It compares a 1991–2020 reference period with 2021–2025 using indicators such as air temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, estimated reference evapotranspiration (ET0), and extreme heat days. ET0 is estimated using the Hargreaves–Samani method. These indicators characterize historical agroclimatic exposure; they are not converted into predicted field yields or irrigation requirements. The DEMATEL module asks the farmer to assess directional influences among five agricultural cost factors: irrigation and energy, agricultural inputs, labor and machinery, climate adaptation, and crop rotation management. Five factors assessed against the other four produce 20 directed pairwise questions. DEMATEL turns these judgments into a structured influence matrix and cause–effect insights, making the farmer’s experience explicit and quantitatively interpretable. The key contribution is the integration of open NASA climate information with transparent economic scenario calculations and farmer-informed systems analysis in one usable interface. The DEMATEL results provide interpretive context; they do not automatically change the economic ranking. The pilot is intended to support discussion and decision exploration and could later be extended to additional crops, regions, and validated field data. Development tools: R, R Shiny, NASA POWER data, DEMATEL-based calculations, and deployment on shinyapps.io.
